description:
Programme or Project Overview

The Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics at Stockholm University invites applications for a PhD student position in bioinformatics. The position develops computational approaches to biological data, working across large-scale sequencing, proteomics or imaging datasets depending on the project line, and contributing methods that the department's experimental groups rely on. The employment is a salaried four-year doctoral contract under the Swedish collective agreement, based in Stockholm's dense molecular life-science environment.

Bioinformatics research at the department connects algorithm development with biological interpretation: candidates typically build pipelines and statistical models, validate them against experimental data and collaborate directly with wet-lab colleagues. Stockholm University hosts strong national infrastructure for data-intensive life science, and doctoral students benefit from training programmes in computational biology, close links to Science for Life Laboratory and an international seminar culture.

Candidate profile

Applicants hold a master's degree in bioinformatics, computational biology, computer science or a life-science field with strong computational experience. Solid programming skills and familiarity with statistics are expected; experience with genomics data or machine learning is an advantage. Applications run through Stockholm University's Varbi system with a CV, transcripts, references and a motivation letter, and selection emphasises both technical skill and biological curiosity.

Highlights

  • Salaried four-year PhD employment in bioinformatics
  • Computational methods for large-scale biological data
  • Direct collaboration with experimental groups
  • National data-infrastructure and SciLifeLab links
  • Machine learning and statistical modelling experience valued
  • Application via the Varbi recruitment system

About Stockholm University

Stockholm University is a public research university in the Swedish capital with roughly 30,000 students and a strong research profile in the natural sciences, psychology, humanities, law and social sciences. Many of its departments collaborate with national research institutes located on the same campus areas, including the neighbouring Science for Life Laboratory environment. Doctoral students in Sweden are employed on paid contracts with collective-agreement salaries and full social benefits. PhD and postdoctoral vacancies are recruited through the national Varbi system used by Swedish universities.
